rv.q: His great feat is to make every scene legible, without, for the most part, sacrificing the rhythm of the play.
Baldwin and the Red Bull Theater have achieved this latter result with a Richard II that leverages its chic, modern trappings to offer a striking vision of Shakespeare's most poetic king.
Urie brilliantly embodies Shakespeare's King Richard, infusing him with just enough whimsy and vulnerability to make this manchild pitiable.
But if you're on the lookout for something as simple as a Shakespeare production that feels fresh and stirring, this play's the thing.

Herein lies the production's greatest strength, Richard's clinging to the belief that the throne is his by divine right, and that whatever has befallen him is an affront to God as much as to his royal self, a nepo baby of his time. There is a certain amount of youthful petulance in his actions, befi...

Despite some pretty speeches and piquant philosophical musings, it’s just not that compelling a story. Luckily for director-adapter Craig Baldwin, Richard is portrayed by Michael Urie, who proves to be just as adept at tragedy as comedy (sometimes employing both here) and gives a transfixing performance that gains our sympathy.
The only time this production really breathes is when Urie is alone in that giant glass box.
Urie never aspires to majesty and hence never achieves it.
But this Richard II emerges more as an exercise in style than substance, unable to justify why its 1980s glosses enhance our understanding of this story or these characters.
